questions.question: Walk through Mono and Flux — their operators, schedulers, and practical use.
questions.title: Mono and Flux — Operators, Schedulers, and Practical Use
questions.direct_answer: **`Mono<T>`** represents 0 or 1 async result; **`Flux<T>`** represents 0..N async results. Both are Reactive Streams `Publisher`s and are **cold by default** — nothing happens until you subscribe. Composition is via operators in four families: transforming (`map`, `flatMap`, `zip`), error-handling (`onErrorResume`, `retryWhen`), combining (`merge`, `concat`, `switchMap`), and scheduling (`subscribeOn`, `publishOn`, `timeout`). **Schedulers** pick the thread pool: `parallel()` for CPU, `boundedElastic()` for blocking, `single()` for serial, `immediate()` for caller. Golden rules: use `flatMap` (not `map`) when the transform returns another `Mono`/`Flux`; never block on event-loop threads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Concrete reactive operator usage, scheduler selection, practical patterns and pitfalls
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using map instead of flatMap; blocking in reactive chain; misunderstanding cold vs hot; forgetting to subscribe
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss operator fusion, backpressure propagation, groupBy semantics, checkpoint for debugging, parallel Flux for CPU pipelines

sections.title: Mono and Flux — The Two Core Types
sections.content:
Reactor exposes two `Publisher` types that anchor every reactive API in the Spring ecosystem.

**`Mono<T>`** carries 0 or 1 item then completes (or errors). Think of it as a `Future` that may be empty. Use it for a single async value: a database fetch by id, an HTTP GET, a cache lookup.

**`Flux<T>`** carries 0..N items then completes (or errors). It is a stream. Use it for collections, server-sent events, Kafka consumption, scanning rows.

Both implement Reactive Streams `Publisher<T>`. Both are **cold** by default — the underlying work doesn't begin until somebody subscribes, and each subscriber triggers its own run. That property is what makes reactive pipelines composable: the chain is a description, not an execution.

sections.title: Operators Pipeline — map > filter > flatMap > subscribe
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    src["Source: Flux.range(1, 100)"] --> mapOp["map(i -> i * 2) sync"]
    mapOp --> filterOp["filter(i -> i > 10)"]
    filterOp --> flatOp["flatMap(i -> webClient.fetch(i)) async"]
    flatOp --> dnOp["doOnNext(log) side effect"]
    dnOp --> subOp["subscribe(consumer) triggers the chain"]
    subOp -.request 256.-> flatOp
    flatOp -.request.-> filterOp
    filterOp -.request.-> mapOp
    mapOp -.request.-> src
```

sections.title: Creating and Consuming Mono / Flux
Operators You Will Use Daily
sections.content:
**Transforming**
- `map(fn)` — synchronous 1-to-1 transform
- `flatMap(fn)` — `fn` returns a `Mono` / `Flux`; runs asynchronously
- `flatMapMany` — `Mono<T>` to `Flux<R>`
- `flatMapSequential` — preserves outer order at buffering cost
- `concatMap` — one inner at a time, in order

**Filtering**
- `filter(predicate)`, `take(n)`, `takeUntil`, `takeWhile`
- `skip(n)`, `skipUntil`, `skipWhile`, `distinct()`

**Combining**
- `Flux.merge(a, b)` — interleave items as they arrive
- `Flux.concat(a, b)` — strict order: a fully, then b
- `Mono.zip(a, b)` / `Flux.zip(a, b)` — wait for all, combine into tuple
- `combineLatest` — emit combined whenever any source emits
- `switchMap` — switch to latest inner, cancel previous (search-as-you-type)
- `window` / `buffer` — time- or count-based chunks
- `groupBy` — split into `Flux` of sub-`Flux` by key

**Error handling**
- `onErrorReturn(fallback)` — substitute a value
- `onErrorResume(err -> Mono.just(fallback))` — substitute a publisher
- `onErrorContinue` — skip and continue (use carefully)
- `retry(n)` / `retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...))`
- `doOnError` — side effect; doesn't transform
- `timeout(Duration)` — fail if too slow

**Side effects (debugging / logging)**
- `doOnNext` / `doOnError` / `doOnSubscribe` / `doOnCancel` / `doOnTerminate` / `doFinally`
- `log()` — logs all signals
- `checkpoint("label")` — tags position for stack-trace context

**Time-based**
- `delayElements(d)`, `delaySubscription(d)`, `interval(d)`, `take(Duration)`

**Scheduling**
- `subscribeOn(scheduler)` — affects upstream source
- `publishOn(scheduler)` — switches downstream operators

**Realistic chain example**

```java
public Mono<OrderDto> buildOrderDto(String orderId) {
    return orderRepo.findById(orderId)
        .flatMap(order -> Mono.zip(
            customerClient.byId(order.customerId())
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
                .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Customer.anonymous())),
            lineRepo.findByOrderId(order.id()).collectList(),
            shippingClient.trackingFor(order.id())
                .defaultIfEmpty(Tracking.none()))
            .map(t -> toDto(order, t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())))
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new OrderNotFound(orderId)))
        .checkpoint("after buildOrderDto");
}
```

sections.title: Schedulers — Where Work Actually Runs
sections.content:
By default, Reactor operators run on the calling thread. `subscribeOn` and `publishOn` change that.

**Built-in schedulers**
- `Schedulers.parallel()` — fixed pool sized to CPUs; CPU-bound non-blocking work
- `Schedulers.boundedElastic()` — expandable pool with upper bound; wraps blocking I/O
- `Schedulers.single()` — single reusable thread; serial background tasks
- `Schedulers.immediate()` — runs on the caller's thread
- `Schedulers.fromExecutorService(es)` — bring your own pool

**`subscribeOn` vs `publishOn`**
- `subscribeOn` decides where the source subscription runs; affects everything upstream of that point; first one in the chain wins
- `publishOn` switches the scheduler for operators downstream of that point; can appear multiple times in a chain

```java
source
    .map(this::pureTransform)
    .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel())
    .map(this::cpuBoundTransform)
    .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())
    .map(this::blockingCall)
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
```

**Wrapping blocking code**
- Required pattern when you must call JDBC, blocking HTTP, or legacy libraries from a reactive chain

```java
Mono.fromCallable(() -> jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(sql, Foo.class))
    .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
```

**Never** run blocking code on `parallel()` or the Netty event loop. **BlockHound** in tests catches accidental blocking calls.

**Context propagation — replacing ThreadLocal**
- `Mono.deferContextual` reads the current Reactor `Context`
- `contextWrite` writes into it
- Without this, MDC and Spring Security `SecurityContext` are lost across thread hops
- Spring Boot 3.x bridges Reactor `Context` and MDC via Micrometer Context Propagation

```java
return Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> {
        String tenant = ctx.get("tenant");
        return fetchDataForTenant(tenant);
    })
    .contextWrite(Context.of("tenant", currentTenant()));
```

**Parallel Flux for CPU pipelines**

```java
Flux.range(1, 1000)
    .parallel(4)
    .runOn(Schedulers.parallel())
    .map(this::cpuHeavy)
    .sequential()
    .subscribe(...);
```

Useful for genuinely CPU-parallel pipelines; rare in I/O-bound services.

sections.title: Gotchas, Best Practices, and the Mental Model
sections.content:
**When reactive helps:**
- High-concurrency I/O with truly reactive downstreams
- Streaming with explicit backpressure
- Composing many async calls in one pipeline

**When it hurts:**
- Mixing blocking JDBC into a reactive chain without `boundedElastic` — stalls the event loop
- Heavy `synchronized` regions; reactive code paths can't help with lock contention
- CPU-bound workloads — reactive doesn't make them faster
- Teams without 6+ months of Reactor experience — debugging cost is real

**Watch for — top gotchas:**
- **`map` vs `flatMap`** — use `map` when sync returns plain value; `flatMap` when it returns `Mono`/`Flux`. Wrong choice gives `Mono<Mono<T>>`.
- **Forgetting to subscribe** — cold publishers do nothing until subscribed. WebFlux subscribes for controller returns; background work needs explicit `.subscribe()`.
- **Blocking without scheduler** — `jdbc.query` in a reactive chain stalls the event loop. Always wrap in `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic())`.
- **`Mono.just(expensiveCall())`** — `expensiveCall()` runs eagerly at chain construction. Use `Mono.fromCallable(...)` for lazy evaluation.
- **Cold publisher re-subscribed** — each subscribe re-runs the source. For DB queries, use `.cache()` or `Flux.share()` to share results.
- **Backpressure mismatch** — fast source into slow consumer without backpressure = memory explosion. Use `onBackpressureBuffer/Drop/Latest` with bounds.
- **Error signals terminate the sequence** — once an error fires, the chain ends. `onErrorResume` keeps it going.
- **Thread-hopping surprises** — operators after `publishOn` run on a new scheduler; keep track for transactional or context-sensitive code.
- **`@Transactional` doesn't just work** — use `TransactionalOperator` and reactive transaction managers; R2DBC has reactive transactions.
- **Lazy vs eager** — `Mono.just(x)` captures eagerly; `Mono.fromSupplier` and `Mono.defer` are lazy and fresh per subscribe.

**Operator fusion**
- Reactor optimizes some sync operator chains (`map` + `filter`) for efficiency
- You rarely think about it but knowing it exists explains some performance wins

**Debugging techniques**
- `.log()` — logs every signal
- `.checkpoint("label")` — readable tag in stack traces
- `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` — captures stack trace at each operator (dev only; slow)
- BlockHound — catches accidental blocking on event-loop in tests
- Reactor Tools agent — async stack traces in production

**Testing with `StepVerifier`**

```java
StepVerifier.create(myMono)
    .expectNext("hello")
    .expectComplete()
    .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5));

StepVerifier.create(myFlux)
    .expectNextCount(10)
    .expectErrorMatches(t -> t instanceof MyException)
    .verify();
```

Use `StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(...)` to test `delay` / `interval` operators without waiting in real time.

**The mental model:** *`Mono` / `Flux` is a description; nothing runs until subscribe; operators add behavior; schedulers decide which thread runs what.*

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Mono<T>` = 0 or 1**, **`Flux<T>` = 0..N** async results; both are Reactive Streams `Publisher`
- **Cold by default** — nothing runs until subscribe; each subscribe re-runs the source
- **`flatMap` for async transforms**; `map` for sync; `concatMap` for ordered; `switchMap` for cancel-and-restart
- **Schedulers** — `parallel` (CPU), `boundedElastic` (blocking I/O), `single` (serial), `immediate` (caller)
- **`subscribeOn` affects upstream** source; **`publishOn` switches downstream** operators
- **Never block on event loop** — wrap with `boundedElastic`; BlockHound catches accidents
- **Context propagation** replaces ThreadLocal across threads; Micrometer bridges MDC
- **Error signals terminate** — `onErrorResume` keeps going; `onErrorContinue` is risky
- **Use `.checkpoint()` and `.log()`** for debugging; `Hooks.onOperatorDebug()` in dev
- **Test with `StepVerifier`** including virtual time for delay-based pipelines

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`Mono<T>` is 0 or 1 async result; `Flux<T>` is 0 to N. Both are Reactive Streams `Publisher`s and are cold by default — nothing happens until subscribe.

**Operators by family**
- Transforming: `map` for sync, `flatMap` for async, `concatMap` for ordered, `switchMap` for cancel-and-restart
- Filtering: `filter`, `take`, `skip`, `distinct`
- Combining: `merge` interleaves, `concat` is strictly ordered, `zip` waits for all, `groupBy` splits by key
- Error handling: `onErrorReturn`, `onErrorResume`, `retryWhen` with backoff, `timeout`
- Side effects: `doOnNext`, `log()`, `checkpoint(label)` for debugging
- Scheduling: `subscribeOn`, `publishOn`

**Schedulers**
- `parallel()` — CPU-bound non-blocking, sized to CPUs
- `boundedElastic()` — wrap blocking I/O
- `single()` — serial background
- `immediate()` — caller thread
- Never run blocking code on `parallel()` or Netty event loop

**`subscribeOn` vs `publishOn`**
- `subscribeOn` affects where the source subscription runs; first wins
- `publishOn` switches scheduler for downstream operators; can appear multiple times

**Context propagation**
- Reactor `Context` plus Micrometer Context Propagation bridges MDC and `SecurityContext` across thread hops

**Golden rules**
- Use `flatMap` not `map` when transform returns `Mono` / `Flux`
- Never block on event-loop threads
- Propagate context with Reactor `Context`
- Add `.checkpoint()` and `.log()` when debugging

**Top gotchas**
- `Mono.just(expensiveCall())` runs eagerly; use `Mono.fromCallable` for lazy
- Cold publisher re-subscribed re-runs the source; use `.cache()` for sharing
- `@Transactional` is thread-bound; need `TransactionalOperator` for reactive
- Backpressure mismatch causes memory explosion; bound buffers

**Mental model**
- `Mono` / `Flux` is a description, nothing runs until subscribe, operators add behavior, schedulers decide which thread runs what
- If you're constantly fighting reactive, consider whether virtual threads fit better

questions.question: Mono vs Flux — when do you use each, and what are the common conversion patterns?
questions.title: Mono vs Flux — Choosing the Right Type and Converting Between Them
questions.direct_answer: Pick **`Mono<T>`** when an operation produces at most one value — a single DB lookup, an HTTP GET that returns one resource, an aggregate of multiple async calls, or a `Void` completion signal. Pick **`Flux<T>`** when an operation produces many values over time — a streaming HTTP response, paginated DB rows, SSE / WebSocket frames, or a Kafka subscription. The two interconvert: `flux.collectList()` collapses a `Flux<T>` to a `Mono<List<T>>`; `mono.flatMapMany(...)` expands a `Mono<T>` into a `Flux<R>`; `Mono.zip(a, b)` aggregates several Monos. Choosing the wrong type forces awkward conversions and obscures the signal cardinality your API exposes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands cardinality semantics, how the two types interoperate, and how the type choice shapes the API contract
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning Flux when only one value is produced; calling collectList() inside a chain unnecessarily; using block() to convert types
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Mono<Void> for fire-and-forget, Mono<ResponseEntity<Flux<T>>> for streaming responses, and how cardinality maps to HTTP semantics

sections.title: Cardinality Drives the Choice
sections.content:
The choice between `Mono` and `Flux` is fundamentally about **cardinality** — how many values can the operation produce.

**`Mono<T>` carries 0 or 1.** Use it for single-result operations: a `findById`, an HTTP GET returning one resource, an authentication check, an aggregate computed from multiple async sources. `Mono<Void>` is the idiomatic way to signal completion of a side effect (a write, a publish) with no payload.

**`Flux<T>` carries 0..N.** Use it for streaming operations: a paginated DB scan, server-sent events, WebSocket frames, Kafka consumption, file streaming, anything where the count is unknown or large.

This cardinality is **part of your API contract**. Returning `Flux<User>` when there is exactly one user forces every consumer to call `.next()` or `.singleOrEmpty()` and obscures intent. Returning `Mono<List<User>>` when you actually have a stream of millions of users defeats backpressure and pulls everything into memory.

sections.title: Mono vs Flux — Decision Matrix
sections.content:
Use the cardinality of the operation as your primary signal. The right hand column shows common conversions when you genuinely need one type from the other.

| Use case | Right type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `findById` | `Mono<T>` | empty Mono if not found |
| `findAll` paginated | `Flux<T>` | preserve streaming |
| `findAll` small fixed list | `Flux<T>` or `Mono<List<T>>` | prefer Flux for consistency |
| Single HTTP GET | `Mono<T>` | use `WebClient.bodyToMono` |
| Streaming HTTP response | `Flux<T>` | `bodyToFlux` + SSE |
| Aggregate of N async calls | `Mono<Tuple>` via `Mono.zip` | one combined result |
| Fire-and-forget side effect | `Mono<Void>` | signals completion |
| SSE endpoint | `Flux<ServerSentEvent>` | infinite stream |
| Kafka subscription | `Flux<Record>` | infinite stream |
| Aggregation of stream | `Mono<Result>` | use `reduce` / `collectList` |
| Counting elements | `Mono<Long>` | `flux.count()` |
| Existence check | `Mono<Boolean>` | `flux.hasElements()` |

sections.title: Conversion Patterns Between Mono and Flux
sections.content:
The two types interconvert through a small number of well-known operators.

**`Flux<T>` to `Mono<List<T>>`**
- `collectList()` — collects everything into a list (memory-bound; only for small / bounded streams)
- `collectMap(keyFn)` — collects into a map
- `reduce(seed, fn)` — folds into a single result
- `count()` — `Mono<Long>` of element count
- `hasElements()` — `Mono<Boolean>`
- `next()` — `Mono<T>` of the first element
- `single()` — `Mono<T>`, errors if not exactly one
- `singleOrEmpty()` — `Mono<T>`, errors if more than one

```java
Mono<List<User>> all = userRepo.findAll().collectList();
Mono<Long> count = userRepo.findAll().count();
Mono<User> first = userRepo.findAll().next();
```

**`Mono<T>` to `Flux<R>`**
- `flatMapMany(fn)` — `fn` returns a `Flux`
- `flux()` — wraps the single value as a one-element `Flux`
- `Flux.from(mono)` — generic adapter

```java
Mono<UserId> idMono = ...;
Flux<Order> orders = idMono.flatMapMany(id -> orderRepo.findByUser(id));
```

**Combining multiple Monos into one Mono**
- `Mono.zip(a, b)` — wait for both, combine into `Tuple2`
- `Mono.zip(a, b, c)` — up to 8
- `Mono.when(...)` — completes when all complete; returns `Mono<Void>`

```java
Mono<UserDto> dto = Mono.zip(
        userRepo.findById(id),
        prefRepo.findByUser(id),
        statsClient.fetch(id))
    .map(t -> toDto(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));
```

**Mono<Void> for fire-and-forget**

```java
public Mono<Void> publishEvent(Event event) {
    return kafkaSender.send(Mono.just(SenderRecord.create(...)))
        .then();
}
```

sections.title: Streaming Response Patterns in WebFlux
Pitfalls and Strategic Choices
sections.content:
**When choosing the right type helps:**
- The API contract communicates cardinality at compile time
- Backpressure works end-to-end for streaming endpoints
- Memory stays bounded even with very large datasets
- Consumers don't have to defensively call `.next()` or `.singleOrEmpty()`

**When the wrong choice hurts:**
- `Mono<List<T>>` for a million rows pulls everything into memory before responding
- `Flux<User>` for a single-result `findById` forces awkward consumer code and loses the not-found semantics of `Mono.empty()`
- Mixing the two unnecessarily through repeated `collectList`/`flatMapMany` makes pipelines hard to read

**Watch for:**
- **`collectList()` on an unbounded `Flux`** — silent memory blow-up; only acceptable for known-small results
- **`block()` to convert** — defeats reactive entirely; almost never the right answer in a reactive service
- **`Mono<Flux<T>>`** — usually a sign of misuse; flatten with `flatMapMany` instead
- **`Mono<List<T>>` on a streaming endpoint** — kills SSE / NDJSON streaming; use `Flux<T>` directly
- **Returning `Flux` for a count** — the right type is `Mono<Long>` via `flux.count()`
- **Mixing `Mono<Void>` and explicit empty Mono** — pick a convention per service

**Strategic choices:**
- For new endpoints, decide cardinality first, then pick the type
- For streaming endpoints, set `produces` to NDJSON or SSE to opt into streaming serialization
- For aggregation, prefer `Mono.zip` over manual chaining of `flatMap`
- For very small known-bounded collections, `Mono<List<T>>` is acceptable for ergonomics
- For large or unbounded collections, `Flux<T>` is the only correct choice

**Cardinality and HTTP semantics**
- 200 + body — `Mono<T>`
- 200 + empty list — `Flux<T>` that completes empty
- 204 No Content — `Mono<Void>` returned from a `ResponseEntity` builder
- 404 Not Found — `Mono.empty()` mapped to `switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...))`
- Streaming response — `Flux<T>` with appropriate `produces`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cardinality drives the choice** — `Mono` for 0..1, `Flux` for 0..N
- **`Mono<Void>`** is the idiomatic fire-and-forget completion signal
- **`Flux<T>` to `Mono<List<T>>`** via `collectList()`; only safe for bounded streams
- **`Mono<T>` to `Flux<R>`** via `flatMapMany`
- **`Mono.zip`** aggregates multiple Monos into one combined result
- **`collectList()` on unbounded `Flux`** is a silent memory blow-up
- **`Mono<Flux<T>>`** is almost always a smell — flatten it
- **Streaming endpoints** require `Flux<T>` plus NDJSON or SSE `Content-Type`
- **`Mono.empty()`** maps cleanly to 404 via `switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...))`
- **`block()` to convert types** defeats reactive — almost never the right answer

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Cardinality drives the choice. `Mono` for 0 or 1, `Flux` for 0 to N.

**When to pick each**
- `Mono` for `findById`, single HTTP GET, aggregate of N async calls, fire-and-forget side effects (`Mono<Void>`)
- `Flux` for streaming HTTP, paginated DB scans, SSE / WebSocket frames, Kafka subscriptions, file streaming

**Conversions**
- `flux.collectList()` → `Mono<List<T>>` — only for bounded results
- `mono.flatMapMany(fn)` → `Flux<R>` — expand a single value into a stream
- `Mono.zip(a, b, ...)` — combine multiple Monos into a tuple
- `Mono.when(...)` — wait for many to complete, return `Mono<Void>`
- `flux.count()` / `flux.hasElements()` — aggregate to a single Mono

**WebFlux endpoint patterns**
- Single resource → `Mono<T>` with `application/json`
- Collection materialized → `Flux<T>` with `application/json`
- True streaming → `Flux<T>` with NDJSON or SSE `Content-Type`
- Side-effect with no body → `Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>>`
- Not found → `Mono.empty()` plus `switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(NotFoundException))`

**Pitfalls to call out**
- `collectList()` on unbounded Flux silently blows memory
- `Mono<List<T>>` on a streaming endpoint kills NDJSON / SSE
- `Mono<Flux<T>>` is almost always a misuse; flatten it
- `block()` to convert defeats reactive entirely

**Strategic point**
- Cardinality is part of your API contract
- Picking the right type at the start avoids awkward conversions later
- It also maps cleanly to HTTP semantics — single resource, collection, streaming, no content
